body: Put the request through the front door first. The interesting part is not what the parser makes of "fruit fly" -- it is what it makes of "lives longer", which is the entire request.

the organism is named (fruit fly) and placed as Drosophila melanogaster, and the REQUIREMENT is not read at all: 0 criteria. "Lives longer" is not in the spec vocabulary, so the clause stays unparsed. That is correct behaviour and it is the whole finding: there is no scenario, no metric and no threshold anywhere in this engine for how long an organism lives.

detail.a_bug_this_run_found: Before this run the same sentence produced a GLIDE criterion. familyGlide matches the free-standing word "fly", `fruit fly` contains one, and the parser read the name of the animal as a requirement that it be able to fly -- a criterion nobody asked for, attached to a request about lifespan. Two-word insect names ending in "fly" are now organism names and are taken out of the clause before the criterion families read it.

why: is there any scenario that measures a lifespan?

body: 12 scenario modules exist and 0 of them measure anything like a lifespan: none. The scenarios are glide, current, temperature, depth, altitude, predator, grip and the rest -- every one of them a question asked of an organism at an age, not a question about how many ages it gets. The engine has growth tracks (ontogeny.json, for two teleosts) and no senescence model for anything. There is no mortality rate, no survival curve and no cause of death in this repository.

why: walking: the regime and the cycle arithmetic

body: nothing this layer can check contradicts the design. That is NOT a finding that it moves: there is no muscle here, no metabolism, no control and no energy budget, and 2 of the 4 checks are regime indicators that never fail anything.

detail.froude: Equal Froude number is a NECESSARY condition for two animals to move in a dynamically similar way, and later work is explicit that it is not sufficient -- cursorial and non-cursorial mammals do not move similarly at equal Fr. The widely quoted walk-to-run transition at Fr = 0.5 is a human result. Turning any of that into a pass or a fail for an arbitrary clade would be borrowing a threshold across exactly the gap this repository keeps finding and removing, so this check reports the number and stops.

why: flight: and whether the lift coefficient policy refuses an insect

body: PARTLY EVALUATED: 1 of the 2 checks could not be run at all -- lift_carries_the_weight (the question asked is about POWERED flight, and this check cannot answer it. It compares lift with weight at a given airspeed, which is an area question; powered flight is a power question -- whether the flight muscle can supply the induced and profile power through a wingbeat, continuously, at that animal's mass. That needs a coefficient measured through a wingbeat and a muscle power density for the clade, and this repository has neither.). The checks that did run found no contradiction, and a check that did not run is not a check that passed. The flight branch refuses, and the refusal is the right one: the question asked is about POWERED flight, and this check cannot answer it. It compares lift with weight at a given airspeed, which is an area question; powered flight is a power question -- whether the flight muscle can supply the induced and profile power through a wingbeat, continuously, at that animal's mass. That needs a coefficient measured through a wingbeat and a muscle power density for the clade, and this repository has neither.

detail.why_this_is_correct: The repository holds exactly two measured maximum lift coefficients: a stuffed Cypselurus hiraii and a live Petaurus breviceps. An insect at Re of order 100 with a flapping wing is aerodynamically unlike both -- unsteady, with leading-edge vortex lift that a steady coefficient does not represent at all. Returning a number here by borrowing one of the two would be exactly the failure this layer was built to stop.

body: Ecology is the one layer with any purchase here, and only sideways: a longer-lived fly is a fly exposed to predation for longer. The databases cannot tell us the lifespan, but they can tell us what is on record as eating this animal and whether any of it is in the place we are asking about.

why: who else is there, and what is recorded as eating this clade

body: GBIF holds 4,503 occurrence records for Drosophila melanogaster Meigen, 1830, concentrated in KR, US, SE. In Greater Boston GBIF holds 58,684 records; the 10 most-recorded non-Aves species are listed. None of the 29 taxa GloBI records as eating Drosophila melanogaster Meigen, 1830 appear in this box's top 10 by record count. Read that as a gap in two databases before reading it as an empty niche: the box list is truncated, record-ranked and missing every Aves species. No population parameters were declared, so whether this design could establish against what is there has NOT been evaluated. That question needs numbers no occurrence database contains.

detail.recorded_range: GBIF holds 4,503 occurrence records for Drosophila melanogaster Meigen, 1830, concentrated in KR, US, SE.
detail.relationships_note: Grouped from GloBI's own interaction types. 28 taxa recorded eating this clade, 14 recorded parasitising it, 3 in a recorded mutualistic or symbiotic relationship with it, 13 it is recorded hosting. COMPETITION IS NOT AMONG THEM, and that is not an oversight: competition is the one ecological relationship that leaves almost no direct observational trace, because it is two organisms NOT doing something to each other. GloBI records interactions that somebody watched happen. Nobody watches an exclusion. Types this grouping does not recognise, left in "other": hasParasitoid.
detail.predation_pressure: None of the 29 taxa GloBI records as eating Drosophila melanogaster Meigen, 1830 appear in this box's top 10 by record count. Read that as a gap in two databases before reading it as an empty niche: the box list is truncated, record-ranked and missing every Aves species.
detail.the_sideways_point: GloBI records real predators of this clade with studies behind them. What it cannot give is a predation RATE, and a lifespan question needs a rate: an organism that lives twice as long in a jar may live no longer at all in a place where something eats it every week. The layer supplies the list and refuses the rate.

asked: where this clade is recorded and what is recorded as eating it
what_it_taught: 29 taxa are on record as eating this clade -- damselflies, orb-weavers, dragonflies, bush-crickets -- each traceable to a study. That is the nearest this system gets to the question, and it is not very near: a list of predators is not a mortality rate, and without a rate a longer intrinsic lifespan is not a longer life.
